Female Long snouted barb reach a maximum total length of 25 cm [Li = 25 cm], a size that places them among the larger members of the genus Puntius within their native range. This ultimate length is attained relatively slowly, reflecting the species’ moderately paced growth trajectory typical of many tropical cyprinids inhabiting riverine systems with seasonal food availability. The asymptotic size of females contrasts notably with the substantially smaller dimension recorded at the onset of reproductive capability. Field studies have consistently shown that individuals begin to mature at a total length of 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm], a threshold that marks the transition from the sub-adult phase to physiological readiness for spawning. This size at puberty is achieved during the second year of life under optimal conditions, after which growth continues but at a reduced rate as energetic resources become increasingly partitioned toward gonadal development. The disparity between length at puberty and ultimate length underscores an extended period of post-maturation growth that allows females to maximize fecundity with advancing age and body size.

Reproductive output in this species is closely tied to female body size, and the wet weight at puberty for females has been estimated at 17.7 g [Wwp = 17.7 g], a value derived from length-weight relationships specific to the population. This mass at first maturity represents a critical energetic investment point; individuals must accumulate sufficient somatic reserves to support both the metabolic demands of gonadal recrudescence and the subsequent spawning events typical of an iteroparous life history. As females continue to grow beyond this pubertal stage, their body mass increases substantially, culminating in an ultimate wet weight for females of 161.4 g [Wwi = 161.4 g] at the maximum recorded total length. This nearly tenfold increase in mass from puberty to full adulthood illustrates the considerable scope for somatic expansion that characterizes this cyprinid. The length-mass relationship underlying these values follows a near-cubic scaling pattern, consistent with the general allometric expectations for benthic-feeding freshwater teleosts that maintain a fusiform body shape throughout life.

The earliest life stages of Puntius dorsalis begin with remarkable economy of matter. Fertilised ova have a mean diameter of approximately 1 millimeter, and from this modest starting point the yolk-sac larva emerges at a wet weight at birth of 0.00052 g [Wwb = 0.00052 g]. This extremely low neonatal mass is typical of small-bodied cyprinids that produce numerous, small eggs as part of a broadcast spawning strategy. The eggs themselves are adhesive and demersal, attaching to submerged vegetation where they undergo embryogenesis. After eclosion, the yolk-sac larva remains entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves for the first few days of life, during which time the mouth is still unformed and the larva exists in a non-feeding, lecithotrophic state. The small size at hatching necessitates rapid development of feeding structures, as the point of no return is reached quickly if exogenous prey is not encountered shortly after yolk absorption completes the trophic switch to active feeding. This strategy trades high fecundity for minimal per-offspring investment.

Longevity records for the long snouted barb, derived from mark-recapture studies conducted in Sri Lankan river systems, indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 2,372 days [am = approximately 2,372 days] under natural thermal regimes averaging 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This places P. dorsalis among the longer-lived members of the Puntius complex and suggests a life history strategy that balances moderate annual reproductive output with extended adult survivorship. The relatively warm, stable water temperatures characteristic of the lowland perennial streams this species inhabits likely contribute to sustained metabolic activity across multiple breeding seasons. Age determination from otolith annuli has corroborated the maximum longevity estimate, revealing that very few individuals survive beyond their seventh year. Mortality appears to increase sharply after the fifth breeding season, with senescence manifesting as reduced condition factor and declining fecundity in the oldest age classes.

Comparing the size parameters across the life history of Puntius dorsalis reveals a coherent pattern of allocation between growth and reproduction. The total length at puberty of 12 cm [Lp = 12 cm] is less than half the ultimate total length for females of 25 cm [Li = 25 cm], indicating that this species adopts a strategy of maturation at a relatively small size followed by substantial post-pubertal growth. This pattern is common among iteroparous freshwater fishes that face moderate predation pressure, as early maturity increases the probability of reproducing at least once before mortality intervenes. The body mass trajectory mirrors this length-based schedule: females gain over 140 grams (161.4 g) [Wwi = 161.4 g] between puberty and asymptotic size, an increase that supports a corresponding rise in clutch mass with advancing age. The hatchling mass of 0.00052 g [Wwb = 0.00052 g] stands in stark contrast to the adult mass, illustrating the prodigious growth multiplier of roughly 310,000-fold that occurs over the species’ lifespan of 2,372 days [am = 2,372 days] at 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This ontogenetic trajectory is consistent with a life history that emphasizes early reproduction combined with continued somatic investment.
